name: Al-Mumtaḥanah
meaning: She Who Is Examined or The Woman Tested (Al-Mumtahanah)
revelation_details: Madinan (Revealed post-Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, around 7-8 AH, dealing with national security, shifting alliances, and community boundaries)
core_theme: The ultimate parameters of loyalty and disavowal (Al-Wala' wal-Bara'), separating faith from tribal ties, the legal status of migrating believing women, and establishing just, ethical principles for relations with non-Muslims.
name_origin:
The Surah derives its name, Al-Mumtahanah ("She Who Is Examined"), directly from the tenth verse, which established a crucial judicial screening process for women escaping Makkah.

The Dilemma of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah

In the year 6 AH, the Muslims signed the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah with the Quraysh. One clause stipulated that any man fleeing Makkah to join the Muslims in Madinah must be sent back to the pagans.

Shortly after, a believing woman named Ummu Kulthum bint Uqbah escaped Makkah and arrived in Madinah. Her brothers arrived shortly after, demanding her return under the terms of the treaty. The Prophet (pbuh) was placed in a difficult situation.

The Divine Intervention and Examination

Allah revealed Verse 10 to resolve this legal crisis:

• "O you who have believed, when the believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them (famta-hinu-hun); Allah is most knowing as to their faith. And if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers..."*

The "Examining" Process

The Prophet (pbuh) was commanded to test these incoming women to verify their true intentions. According to classical commentators like Ibn Abbas (ra), the examination required them to take an oath confirming:

• They did not leave home out of hatred for their husbands.
• They did not leave out of a desire for a new worldly environment or a love for Madinah.
• They migrated purely out of love for Allah and His Messenger.

The Legal Resolution

Because the treaty text explicitly mentioned men returning, Allah exempted women from being handed back to abusive or hostile pagan families, as a woman returning to Makkah would be completely unprotected and forced to recant her faith. The financial equity was balanced by ordering the Muslims to repay the pagan ex-husbands the dower (Mahr) they had originally spent.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Limits of Kinship and the Leak of State Secrets
verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
The Surah opens with a strong, urgent command: "O you who have believed, do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies, extending to them affection while they have disbelieved in what came to you of the truth." This refers historically to Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a companion who attempted to secretly warn the Makkans of the Prophet's (pbuh) military plans to protect his vulnerable family in Makkah.
Allah warns that if the enemies of Islam gain the upper hand, they will treat the believers with open hostility, stretching out their hands and tongues with evil, desiring that they would apostatize. Allah places worldly relationships in their proper perspective: "Neither your relatives nor your children will benefit you on the Day of Resurrection; He will judge between you.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Hatib's story is a deeply humanizing narrative about the pressure of family love. Under extreme stress, even a sincere believer can compromise their principles out of fear for their loved ones. However, Allah uses this incident to teach a timeless lesson: when we compromise moral truths or communal safety to secure the worldly futures of our families, we fall into a spiritual trap. True protection is from Allah alone, and on the Day of Judgment, our family ties will be severed; only our moral record will stand.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Model of Ibrahim and the Great Prayer
verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
To guide the believers in navigating complex social separations, Allah points to the ultimate historical precedent: "There has already been for you an excellent pattern in Ibrahim and those with him." Ibrahim and his followers stood before their polytheistic families and declared: "Indeed, we are disassociated from you and from whatever you worship other than Allah. We have denied you, and there has appeared between us and you animosity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone."
The only exception was Ibrahim's promise to ask forgiveness for his father, which was a specific commitment he made before realizing his father was a persistent enemy of God. Ibrahim and his followers turned to Allah with a profound, vulnerable prayer: "Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have returned, and to You is the destination. Our Lord, make us not [objects of] trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Ibrahim is presented as an "excellent pattern" (Uswatun Hasanah) because he prioritized his spiritual mission over tribal bloodlines. The prayer "do not make us a trial (Fitnah) for those who disbelieve" is highly profound. It is a plea that the believers do not become weak, defeated, or morally corrupted, which would lead the disbelievers to assume they are on the path of truth (reasoning that if Islam were true, its followers would not be degraded or failing). It challenges every generation of believers to live up to the dignity of their faith.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Divine Charter of Tolerance and Justice

points.label: The Peaceful
points.detail: Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes - from being righteous (Tabarroohum) toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.

points.label: The Hostile
points.detail: Allah only forbids you from those who fight you because of religion and expel you from your homes and support the expulsion of others - [forbids] that you make allies of them.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
Lest the believers misunderstand the previous verses as a call for total, aggressive isolation from all non-Muslims, Allah reveals a beautifully balanced diplomatic framework: "Perhaps Allah will put, between you and those to whom you have been enemies among them, affection."
Allah then establishes a golden rule for interfaith relations:
1. The Peaceful: "Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes - from being righteous (Tabarroohum) toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly."
2. The Hostile: "Allah only forbids you from those who fight you because of religion and expel you from your homes and support the expulsion of others - [forbids] that you make allies of them.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: These verses are the foundational Islamic texts for religious tolerance, coexistence, and human rights. Allah uses the word Birr (righteousness/kindness) to describe the treatment of peaceful non-Muslims - the exact same word used for the highest forms of treatment, such as parental devotion (Birr al-Walidayn). It teaches us that Islam does not mandate hostility based on religious differences, but solely based on active oppression, violence, and injustice. True justice requires treating peaceful neighbors with dignity, regardless of their theology.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Migrant Women and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
Following the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, several women fled Makkah to seek asylum in Medina. The polytheists demanded their return based on the treaty terms. Allah intervenes with a highly specific legal instruction: "O you who have believed, when the believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them (Fam-tahinoohun)." Allah knows best their actual faith; but if the believers find them to be sincere, they must not return them to the disbelievers, as they are no longer lawful marriages.
The believers are told to return the dowers (Mahr) that the pagan husbands had spent on these women, and conversely, if a Muslim wife apostatizes and flees to Makkah, the Muslims should demand their financial dowers back.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: The "examination" of migrating women was a screening process to ensure they fled out of genuine spiritual conviction, rather than marital disputes or financial convenience. This section shows the high level of legal agency and protection Islam granted to women in the 7th-century world. They were not viewed as mere property to be handed back to hostile husbands; rather, their human rights and spiritual liberty were prioritized above state-level peace treaties, even while maintaining financial equity by returning the dowers.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Pledge of Spiritual and Social Ethics
verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
Allah commands the Prophet (pbuh) regarding the protocol for accepting the oath of allegiance (Bay'ah) from women who seek to join the community. The pledge is uniquely built on spiritual, social, and domestic ethics rather than military service:
1. They will not associate anything with Allah (Shirk).
2. They will not steal.
3. They will not commit adultery.
4. They will not kill their children.
5. They will not bring a slander (Buhtan) that they fabricate between their hands and feet (unjustly attributing paternity).
6. They will not disobey the Prophet (pbuh) in what is right (Ma'ruf).
If they agree to these conditions, the Prophet (pbuh) is told to accept their pledge and ask Allah to forgive them.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: While men's pledges in that era often focused on warfare and defense, the women's pledge represents a code of social hygiene for the family structure. By demanding an end to theft, adultery, infanticide, and slander, Islam established a firm framework to protect women's dignity, marital rights, child safety, and social integrity. The clause "do not disobey in what is right" also teaches a profound leadership lesson: even the Prophet (pbuh), who was divinely guided, bound his obedience to what is Ma'ruf (good, just, and reasonable), establishing that absolute obedience belongs only to the truth.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: The Surah closes by returning to its opening warning: "O you who have believed, do not make allies of a people with whom Allah has become angry." These are individuals who have chosen hostility to the truth and have despaired of the Hereafter, just as the disbelievers despair of [the resurrection of] those in the graves.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Despair (Ya's) is the ultimate spiritual death. When a person completely loses hope in the spiritual reality of the Hereafter, they become entirely locked into the physical world. Their morals become purely opportunistic because they believe this life is the only arena of consequence. This final warning urges the believers to align themselves with hope, justice, and the eternal, rather than those who have given up on their own spiritual souls.

stories_in_surah.title: The Female Pledge of Allegiance: Bai'at an-Nisa' (Verse 12)
stories_in_surah.content:
The Surah concludes by cementing the independent spiritual, legal, and political identity of women in the Islamic state through a specific, structured public oath of allegiance (Bay'ah).

The Content of the Pledge

The Prophet (pbuh) was told to accept the allegiance of women based on fundamental ethical and social criteria rather than military service:

• "O Prophet, when the believing women come to you pledging to you that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor will they steal, nor will they commit adultery, nor will they kill their children, nor will they bring a slander they have falsely fabricated... then accept their pledge..."*

Hadith Context

In a narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha (ra) explained how this process was conducted:

• "The Messenger of Allah (pbuh) used to examine the believing women who migrated to him with this verse... Whoever among the believing women accepted these conditions passed the examination. When they agreed, the Prophet (pbuh) would say to them verbally, 'Go, for I have accepted your pledge.' By Allah, the hand of the Messenger of Allah never touched the hand of any woman in a pledge; he only took their pledge verbally."

This public, foundational text granted women an explicit voice and direct accountability within the community, setting an institutional standard for personal integrity, social morality, and independent civic loyalty to the state.

deep_dives.title: The Secret Letter of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah (Verses 1-3)
deep_dives.content:
The Surah opens with a powerful command: "O you who have believed, do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies..." This opening was revealed regarding a critical security breach involving a respected companion of the Prophet (pbuh).

The Historical Context

Before the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet (pbuh) was making secret preparations to march on the city. Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a companion who fought at Badr, wrote a letter to the leaders of Quraysh warning them of the upcoming, covert military deployment. He gave the letter to a traveling woman to deliver secretly to Makkah in exchange for payment.

Hadith Context

In a detailed narration found in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Ali ibn Abi Talib (ra) narrated:

• "The Messenger of Allah (pbuh) sent me, Az-Zubayr, and Al-Miqdad, saying: 'Proceed until you reach Rawdat Khakh. There you will find a woman in a travel litter who has a letter. Take it from her.'"

They caught up with the woman and demanded the letter. When she denied having it, they told her that the Prophet (pbuh) does not lie, and threatened to search her clothes. She then pulled the letter out from the braids of her hair.

When Hatib was brought before the Prophet (pbuh), Umar ibn Al-Khattab (ra) was furious and said, "O Messenger of Allah, let me chop off the head of this hypocrite!"

However, Hatib explained his motive honestly: "Do not be hasty with me. I was a man close to the Quraysh, but I did not belong to their tribe. The other emigrants (Muhajirun) have relatives in Makkah who protect their families and wealth there. Since I lack that tribal protection, I wanted to do them a favor so they might protect my vulnerable family. I did not do this out of disbelief or apostasy."

The Prophet (pbuh) looked at his companions and said, "He has told you the truth." He then reminded Umar of Hatib's past sacrifices: "He participated in Badr. You never know, perhaps Allah looked at the people of Badr and said, 'Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you.'

deep_dives.title: The Ideal Model of Loyalty: The Example of Abraham (Verses 4-6)
deep_dives.content:
To clear up any confusion regarding alliances, Allah directs the believers to a historical, spiritual archetype of clarity: Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim, as).

Setting Boundaries with Love and Justice

The Surah explains that blood relations or children will not benefit anyone on the Day of Judgment if faith is compromised. Believers are told to echo the words of Abraham and his followers when they spoke to their pagan tribesmen:

• "Indeed, we are disassociated from you and from whatever you worship other than Allah. We have denied you, and there has appeared between us and you animosity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone..."* (Verse 4)

The Exception in Abraham's Prayer

The Qur'an notes a vital exception in Abraham's example: his promise to pray for his biological father's forgiveness. However, once it became clear his father was entirely committed to enmity against God, Abraham stopped. The Surah utilizes this to show that ultimate allegiance belongs entirely to the spiritual bond of faith, transcending the biological or tribal ties that dominated Pre-Islamic Arabia.

deep_dives.title: Categories of Coexistence: Just vs. Hostile Non-Muslims (Verses 7-9)
deep_dives.content:
Lest the believers misinterpret the strict separation from hostile pagans as a mandate for absolute, universal hatred against all outsiders, the Surah introduces a highly nuanced legal framework for foreign policy and community relations.

The Divine Distinction

Allah provides a clear, structural binary to guide how Muslims treat non-Muslims, dividing them based on their actions, not simply their beliefs:

• Category of People: Peaceful Non-Muslims (Verse 8) — Divine Instruction: Treat with kindness (Birr) and absolute justice — Conditions/Context: Those who do not fight Muslims because of religion and do not drive them out of their homes.
• Category of People: Hostile Aggressors (Verse 9) — Divine Instruction: Alliance/Intimacy is Forbidden — Conditions/Context: Those who actively wage war against Muslims due to faith, expel them, or aid others in expelling them.

The term used for peaceful non-Muslims - Birr - is the exact same word used for the highest forms of devotion, such as filial piety (Birr al-Walidayn). It shows that justice and social kindness are baseline human obligations owed to anyone who does not initiate violence or persecution against the community.
